facts.text: A hiring slowdown is the credible initiating condition, because most revenue is pre-onboarding screening that depends on hiring volumes. Lower volumes would first reduce revenue and the operating leverage that has lifted Adjusted EBITDA margin, then cut EBITDA faster than cash interest, which does not fall with volumes, so cover would narrow first, prepayments would shrink next and net leverage would rise last. The observable triggers are quarterly revenue growth, Adjusted EBITDA margin and whether the repurchase programme continues. No stress figure is established here. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 32; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 40; calculation C09; calculation C21

rows.label: Chart data: revenue and EBITDA — paragraph 1

limitations: Produced in a host session and accepted by the CP-OS check.
Literal checked analytical handoff, not native contract acceptance; source qualifications and gaps remain.

- High: The acquisition effective 4 November 2026 is described in one paragraph of the third-quarter report. The target is unnamed, and its earnings, the cash it holds, the source of the remaining USD 80.0 million of the USD 125.0 million consideration and the working-capital adjustment are not stated. Post-period net debt, leverage and liquidity are therefore not established, and the 4.19x pro forma net leverage is an upper bound on net debt over unchanged EBITDA. The next quarterly or annual report would close this. Basis: calculation C10; calculation C19; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 23 - Medium: The only printed maturity table is at 31 December 2025. Voluntary prepayments of USD 95.0 million in 2026 reduced later instalments and the issuer does not restate the table, so the wall at 30 September 2026 is not established and the ladder shown is dated. The annual report for 2026 would close this. Basis: calculation C06; calculation C07; calculation C19; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 156–157; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 12 - Medium: Security and guarantees are described only in the 2024 annual report. The later filings do not repeat them and the effect of the July 2025 repricing amendment on them is not established. No executed credit agreement is supplied and the springing first lien net leverage test is known only from the issuer's summary, so no covenant headroom is calculated and the senior secured ratios rest on older evidence. The credit agreement and its amendments would close this. Basis: 10-K_2024-12-31_fa-20241231.htm.jsonl, page 112; 10-K_2024-12-31_fa-20241231.htm.jsonl, page 158; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 12; Source readiness (CP-0) - Medium: The issuer states no unadjusted EBITDA, so EBITDA (Reported) is derived from net income, interest, tax and depreciation and amortization and every reported-basis ratio rests on it. Adjusted EBITDA is issuer-stated, but the add-backs carry no realisation status and the integration, restructuring and other line mixes non-cash and other charges. Component detail of that line would close this. Basis: calculation C03; calculation C04; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 101–102; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 40–41 - Medium: No pro forma EBITDA or debt service is stated for FY2024 or FY2023, only pro forma revenue and net loss for the Sterling acquisition, so FY2024 leverage and cover cannot be restated on a like-for-like perimeter and are flagged not comparable. The FY2025 and last-twelve-months ratios are unaffected because both carry Sterling in full. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 153; 10-K_2024-12-31_fa-20241231.htm.jsonl, page 155; calculation C05 - Low: Income and cash flow statements for FY2022 are printed in the 2024 annual report but were not extracted, and no balance sheet at 2022-12-31 is supplied, so no FY2022 ratio is built. The FY2023 to FY2025 columns cover the pre-acquisition baseline and the acquisition years. Basis: 10-K_2024-12-31_fa-20241231.htm.jsonl, pages 134–135 - Low: Several cash flow lines are printed only in the annual statements (loss on foreign currency exchange rates, acquisitions of businesses, borrowings from and payments of issuance costs on the facility, payments on deferred purchase agreements, cash dividends and finance lease payments), and one line is printed only in the interim statements. The 9M 2025 and 9M 2026 cells for the missing lines are not supplied rather than zero; the section totals still reconcile exactly. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 133–134; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 3–4; calculation C12 - Low: No balance sheet at 2025-09-30, no 2024 interim reports and no discrete quarters are supplied, so no quarterly ratio is built and a fourth quarter of 2025 would be a difference, not a reported figure. Seasonality is therefore not assessed. The 2025 interim reports would close this. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2–4; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 133 - Low: Gross interest expense and interest income are not printed separately on the statements. The 2025 annual report states interest income inside interest expense, net of USD 3.7 million, USD 9.6 million and USD 13.4 million for FY2025, FY2024 and FY2023, and no figure for 2026, so gross-interest cover and unlevered free cash flow are not established. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 139; calculation C19 - Low: Maintenance and growth capital expenditure are not split; capitalized software development is the larger part of the total. Recurring free cash flow after maintenance spending is therefore not established, and levered free cash flow uses total capital expenditure. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 134; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 3; calculation C13 - Low: Revolver availability at 2023-12-31 is not stated, because the 2023 annual report is not supplied, so FY2023 liquidity shows cash only. Restricted cash is excluded from cash and liquidity throughout and is small. Basis: 10-K_2024-12-31_fa-20241231.htm.jsonl, page 157; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 132; calculation C12 - Low: The minimum-volume purchase commitment, the funding duty under the consent decrees and the make-up of the accrued legal liability are not quantified in the filings, so the claims outside debt are bounded by the stated lease, legal and tax items only. No pension, retiree medical, factoring or supply-chain finance obligation was found after searching every source. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 33; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 112; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 19; calculation C22 - Low: Source dashes in the audited statements and in the printed maturity table are read as nil where the printed subtotals and the maturity total tie without them, for example the FY2023 loss on extinguishment, the FY2025 acquisitions line and the 2026 and 2027 maturity rows. This is a reading of the tables, not a stated zero, and a dash that does not tie is left as not supplied. The issuer's own statement of nil amounts would close this. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 133–134; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 157; calculation C06; calculation C12 - Low: The 9M 2026 equity roll-forward differs from reported equity by a printed rounding of a single unit, which does not affect any cash or profit figure. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 4–5; calculation C15 - Low: No numeric operating series such as customers, volumes, retention or backlog is stated in the filings, so the dashboard carries only issuer margins, segment margins, growth and geographic share. The filings describe volumes in words only. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 34; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 32 - Low: No 2025 interim report is supplied, so the 9M 2025 comparatives are taken from the 2026 report and cannot be checked for restatement; the nine-month 2025 figures used to build the last twelve months are as the 2026 report prints them. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 3–4; calculation C05 - Low: The extracted text flattens tables to one cell per line and splits negative figures across lines, so each figure was read from order and checked against its subtotal; every identity reconciles, but a column misreading that preserved a subtotal would not be detected. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2–3; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 133–134

facts.label: Key findings

Silver Lake beneficially owned 51.4% of the common stock at the end of 2025, down from 51.7% a year earlier, and under the stockholders' agreement its approval is needed for debt above USD 100.0 million, joint ventures above USD 100.0 million and a change of control for as long as it holds at least 25%. A large debt-funded acquisition or recapitalisation therefore cannot happen without the sponsor, so financial policy follows the sponsor's view. Creditors rely on the credit agreement for protection, and that agreement is not supplied, so capacity to pay out cash, move assets or prime lenders is not assessed. facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: The business is a high-retention, transactional screening franchise whose revenue still moves with hiring. Gross retention was about 96% in both 2024 and 2025, the customer count stayed in the tens of thousands in both years, and no customer reached 10% of FY2025 revenues, although one customer was about 12% in FY2024 and FY2023. Against that, most revenue is pre-onboarding screening ordered per individual, contracts carry no minimum volumes and customers can leave on short notice without penalty, so a hiring slowdown lowers revenue without any contract being lost. The annual reports state customers, retention, tenure and screens for both years, which corrects the earlier view in Financial foundation that no such series is stated; two years show stable retention but are too short to show a trend. facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Governance disclosure is strong where it is audited and thin where it is incorporated by reference. Statements are audited, with an opinion that they present fairly, and internal control was effective, quarterly reports are filed and no material related-party transactions are reported, but directors, pay and independence sit in a proxy statement that is not supplied. Overall, First Advantage presents medium sponsor and governance risk: the key supported behaviours are the 2023 payout and repeated acquisitions, which matter because they move cash and debt at the sponsor's discretion, and imply that deleveraging is a choice, not a commitment. Countervailing evidence is the voluntary paydown and the stated policy of no dividends. Further analysis requires the proxy statement and the credit agreement. facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against reading sponsor behaviour as mixed, not adverse, is the 2023 special dividend, paid to shareholders of whom Silver Lake is the largest, and the speed with which a new acquisition followed the 2026 paydown; together they suggest cash is returned or redeployed whenever liquidity allows. The view would turn adverse if the company announced a debt-funded dividend or buyback, if a new amendment widened sponsor consent to higher leverage, or if the credit agreement proved to allow wide payouts or asset transfers. It would improve if the proxy statement showed no sponsor fees or related-party payments, if the 2026 target proved modest and low-risk, and if voluntary prepayments continued at the 2026 pace. A fall in Silver Lake's holding below 25% would remove its approval rights and change who decides debt questions. facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: The credit is adequate and improving, but leverage is still close to four times EBITDA. Total debt to reported EBITDA fell from 5.47x at the end of 2025 to 4.45x on the last twelve months to 30 September 2026, and net debt to reported EBITDA from 4.84x to 3.91x at 30 September 2026, which becomes 4.19x pro forma for the acquisition of 4 November 2026. Of the improvement in total leverage, 77.10% came from higher EBITDA and 22.90% from lower debt, and on the issuer's adjusted measure total leverage moved from 4.71x to 4.09x. The pro forma figure counts the full cash consideration and no earnings from the target, so it is an upper bound, and pro forma cash is not established. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation F01; calculation F04

facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against an adequate and improving credit is that part of the improvement comes from lower one-off charges and part is already reversed by the acquisition. Reported EBITDA grew 17.76% against 10.37% for adjusted EBITDA because the charges the issuer adds back shrank, free cash flow converts only 36.39% of adjusted EBITDA, and the acquisition of 4 November 2026 lifts net leverage to 4.19x pro forma from 3.91x before any earnings from the target are counted. The view would be confirmed if net leverage stayed below the 4.84x of end-2025 once the acquisition is consolidated and cover stayed above 2.35x. It would turn negative if reported EBITDA fell 13.43% on a pro forma net debt basis, which returns net leverage to 4.84x, or 25.84%, which returns cover to 2.35x, or if a further debt-funded deal or payout used the liquidity. Basis: calculation F01; calculation F03; calculation F04; calculation F06; Financial foundation (CP-1)

facts.label: Company description
facts.text: First Advantage sells employment background screening and identity verification to employers, covering criminal, education and work-history checks, identity and drug screening, driver and healthcare credentials, continuous monitoring and adjacent products such as fleet compliance and hiring tax credits. Revenue is transactional, since an employer orders a package of checks for one person, so it follows hiring volumes, yet relationships are long, gross retention is about 96% and no customer reached 10% of FY2025 revenues. The United States produces 85.81% of revenues and the Sterling acquisition of October 2024 made Sterling 49.07% of gross segment revenues. For creditors this means cash-flow visibility is good at the relationship level and weak at the volume level, so debt service depends on earnings tracking hiring and refinancing confidence rests on leverage, not on contracted revenue. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation F07

facts.label: Revenue drivers and pricing power
facts.text: Revenue is driven by volumes: most revenue is pre-onboarding screening that follows employer hiring, growth in the nine months to September 2026 came from existing customers at 8.4% and new customers at 4.2%, and the issuer says pricing was relatively stable, so pricing power is not demonstrated. Revenue is recurring in relationship but not in volume, because contracts carry no minimum volumes and customers can end them at short notice. It is cyclical with hiring and exposed to customers taking screening in-house or using AI-driven hiring tools. That means a hiring slowdown reduces revenue without any contract being lost, which is the first break in the downside path. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation F09; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 39; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 34

facts.label: Cost structure and margin resilience
facts.text: Cost of services, which is mostly third-party data, government fees, fulfilment and customer care, is 54.33% of FY2025 revenues, so a large part of cost varies with volume and protects margin when orders fall. The issuer says third-party fees are typically invoiced to customers as pass-through costs, but its risk factors state that fee increases cannot always be passed on, so pass-through is partial. Adjusted EBITDA margin was 28.5% in the nine months to September 2026 against 28.1% a year earlier, with automation and operating leverage credited by management, while the International segment margin fell to 5.95% from 16.12%. Margins can be defended against a moderate volume fall, but technology and overhead costs are largely fixed, so a deeper fall would cut EBITDA faster than revenue. facts.text: The business needs little physical capital but invests continuously in software, and capital expenditure, mostly capitalized software, rose 56.85% in the nine months to September 2026. facts.label: Porter's five forces
facts.text: Rivalry is moderate to high: the market is fragmented, with a limited number of multinational firms, and the issuer competes on accuracy, turnaround, compliance and price, so competitors can force price concessions that would cut margin. New entrants are a live threat from applicant tracking and payroll providers that build screening into their products, which could erode volumes and the integrations that sustain retention. Substitutes are customers insourcing screening and AI-driven hiring tools that lower hiring volumes. Buyer power is high, because customers can leave at short notice, buy from several providers and are often steered by human capital software partners. Supplier power is meaningful, since data providers and laboratories are non-exclusive, some are owned by competitors, and fee increases cannot always be passed on, which pressures margin at the cost-of-services line. facts.label: Downside scenario
facts.text: The initiating condition is a hiring slowdown across retail, transportation and healthcare customers. Orders fall at once because contracts carry no minimum volumes, revenue follows, and EBITDA falls faster than revenue because technology and overhead costs are largely fixed, while cost of services at 54.33% of revenue flexes. Cash interest does not fall with volumes and rises if SOFR rises after the swaps expire, so cover narrows first: a 25.84% fall in reported EBITDA returns cover to 2.35x. Free cash flow then shrinks and prepayments slow, so net leverage rises, and a fall of 13.43% on pro forma net debt returns it to the 4.84x of end-2025. Management levers are to stop buybacks and acquisitions, defer software capex and keep prepaying; liquidity of USD 490.2 million before the acquisition and no principal due before 2028 mean resilience appears sufficient to avoid distress in this scenario, though the buffer and the revolver covenant test above 40.0% use must be watched. Observable triggers are screening volumes, adjusted EBITDA margin, cash after the acquisition and any new payout. citations.quote: The initiating condition is a hiring slowdown across retail, transportation and healthcare customers. Orders fall at once because contracts carry no minimum volumes, revenue follows, and EBITDA falls faster than revenue because technology and overhead costs are largely fixed, while cost of services at 54.33% of revenue flexes. Cash interest does not fall with volumes and rises if SOFR rises after the swaps expire, so cover narrows first: a 25.84% fall in reported EBITDA returns cover to 2.35x. Free cash flow then shrinks and prepayments slow, so net leverage rises, and a fall of 13.43% on pro forma net debt returns it to the 4.84x of end-2025. Management levers are to stop buybacks and acquisitions, defer software capex and keep prepaying; liquidity of USD 490.2 million before the acquisition and no principal due before 2028 mean resilience appears sufficient to avoid distress in this scenario, though the buffer and the revolver covenant test above 40.0% use must be watched. Observable triggers are screening volumes, adjusted EBITDA margin, cash after the acquisition and any new payout.

facts.label: Overall credit view
facts.text: Overall, First Advantage presents an adequate business profile supported by sticky customers, scale among multinational screening firms and ample liquidity, but credit quality is constrained by leverage near four times EBITDA, floating-rate exposure, hiring-driven volumes and a controlling sponsor with an acquisitive record. Cash-flow durability appears adequate: interest is covered 3.17x and free cash flow is positive, but conversion is thin. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on leverage at 2028 and later maturities and on whether the sponsor keeps using cash for deals. The primary downside path is a hiring slowdown that cuts EBITDA faster than revenue while rates rise on unhedged debt. Further analysis would require the credit agreement, ratings and market data, the target and cash after the 2026 acquisition, and the proxy statement. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); Source readiness (CP-0); calculation F01; calculation F02; calculation F03; calculation F05; calculation F07

## Findings
### Bottom line

The five supplied filings support the requested financial foundation, business description and fundamental credit work, but no supplied source gives ratings, traded debt prices or executed loan documents, so any view on instrument choice or covenant terms stays unsupported. The latest quarterly report was signed 13 days before the as-of date and nothing supplied is dated after the cutoff.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 51; calculation C01

The cross-checks run agree: the term loan principal at the end of the third quarter equals the 2025 year-end principal less USD 95.0 million of voluntary prepayments. The only subsequent event the third-quarter report records is the 4 November 2026 acquisition, described in one paragraph with an unnamed target and a USD 45.0 million revolver draw after the balance sheet date, so post-period leverage and liquidity cannot be sized from the filing alone.

## Gaps

- Material: No executed credit agreement, amendment or security document is supplied, and the run settings declare none. The 2025 annual report lists the first lien credit agreement and its amendments among its exhibits, but the terms in the filings, including the springing leverage test, are the issuer's own summaries. Legal & covenants cannot run until an executed document is supplied, and Covenant capacity and Structural priority could use the summaries only, labelled as such.

- Material: The guarantee and collateral description appears only in the 2024 annual report: the facility is guaranteed by the borrower's direct parent and material wholly owned domestic restricted subsidiaries and secured by a first priority security interest in certain assets of the borrower and the guarantors and a first-priority pledge of the stock of the borrower and of its wholly owned material restricted subsidiaries. The four later filings do not repeat it; the 2025 annual report mentions collateral only in a general risk factor. The effect of the July 2025 repricing amendment on it is not established, and Structural priority must label the description as older evidence.

- Material: No credit rating, rating agency or rating date appears in any source; the 2025 annual report says only that the company receives debt ratings from major agencies. Ratings & triggers has no input, and Fundamental credit and Committee decision cannot cite a rating.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 69

- Material: No traded debt price, spread, issue term, peer set or equity quote is supplied. The only market-derived points are the non-affiliate market value at the end of June 2025 on the cover of the 2025 annual report, an average repurchase price of USD 18.17 per share in September 2026 and a cumulative return graph whose values are not carried in the text. Security selection and Market-implied risk cannot run, and Peer benchmark has no peers.

- Material: The acquisition effective 4 November 2026 is described in one paragraph of the third-quarter report: a U.S.-based data platform business and a small employment background screening operation, for USD 125.0 million of cash consideration subject to working capital adjustments, with USD 45.0 million borrowed under the revolver. The target is unnamed, and there are no target financials, purchase agreement or pro forma figures. Financial foundation must keep the event outside the 30 September 2026 figures, and Liquidity and Downside must treat post-period leverage and liquidity as not established unless the filing states them.

- Material: The latest debt maturity table is at 31 December 2025, when no principal fell due before 2028, and the 2026 quarterly reports carry none. The third-quarter report states total principal but no updated table, and USD 95.0 million of voluntary prepayments in 2026 reduced remaining scheduled repayments without a restated schedule. The 30 September 2026 maturity wall must be shown as not stated, or derived from the year-end table and labelled as derived.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 157; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 11–12; calculation C02

- Material: No management case, guidance, earnings release, investor presentation or bridge from reported to forward figures is supplied, and the run settings carry no forward assumptions. Forward credit model cannot run on a management basis, and Downside and Liquidity can use reported history and disclosed terms only.

- Minor: The annual reports incorporate director, executive officer, compensation and related-party information by reference to a proxy statement that is not supplied, so Business & governance rests on the business description, the ownership risk factor and the notes.

- Minor: Discrete fourth quarters are not stated. The fourth quarter of 2025 can be derived as the annual figure less the nine-month 2025 comparative in the third-quarter report, but no 2024 interim report is supplied, so no 2024 quarter can be built. Cash flow statements are year-to-date, so discrete quarterly cash flows are differences and must be labelled as constructions. FY2025 against FY2024 also includes Sterling for twelve months against two months, and pro forma results are supplied for FY2024 and FY2023 only.

- Minor: The extracted text flattens tables to one cell per line, splits negative figures across lines and breaks statements across page boundaries, so column alignment is read from order and each figure needs a check against its subtotal. No chart or image content is carried, for example the stock performance graph.

- Minor: Each document states a signature date and none states a filing date, so signature dates stand in for publication dates. No source covers the 13 days between the latest signature and the as-of date, so any rating action or current report in that window would not appear.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 51; calculation C01
- Minor: No portfolio, fund limit or prior case is supplied, so Committee decision states the fund's limits as not supplied and Changes since the last run has nothing to compare.

- Minor: Total debt has two stated definitions that both tie to the statements: principal of USD 2,019.5 million in the liquidity discussion and carrying value net of deferred financing costs on the balance sheet. The difference is deferred financing costs, and this is a definition difference, not a source conflict. No source conflict was found in the cross-checks run on debt principal, revolver availability and cash.

spans.text: ## Request

First Advantage Corp (issuer fa-1210677), as of 2026-11-18, credit snapshot pathway. Scope: the financial foundation on the five supplied filings, covering the statements for FY2023 to 9M 2026, carrying-value debt, the last twelve months to 2026-09-30, leverage, cover, liquidity and the gaps that limit them.
## Sources
| Source | Document | Document date | sha256 | Use |

| 10-K_2024-12-31_fa-20241231.htm.jsonl | Annual report on Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2024 | 2025-02-27 | 4ef8c67512d96b80980fdff201710b789a26049ecc55b4beb1e0fe105460431f | FY2023 balance sheet; cross-check of FY2024; guarantee and collateral description; debt tables and liquidity at 2024-12-31 |

Document dates are the dates each report states it was signed; no document states a filing date. No external source was used.
## Findings
### Bottom line

Net debt is 3.91x last-twelve-months reported EBITDA at 30 September 2026 and cash interest is covered 3.17x, but a USD 125.0 million cash acquisition on 4 November 2026 lifts net leverage to 4.19x, so deleveraging now depends on earnings growth.
Basis: calculation C09; calculation C10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 23

The FY2024 ratios are not comparable, because year-end debt carries the full Sterling financing while reported EBITDA holds two months of Sterling and USD 125.7 million of its transaction charges. All funded debt is one first lien bank facility with no scheduled principal due before 2028 at the end of 2025, and cash plus the undrawn revolver of USD 490.2 million is 24.62% of total debt.
Basis: calculation C08; calculation C19; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 102; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 157; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 45
### Financial interpretation

Leverage has fallen because earnings rose and debt was repaid. Total debt to reported EBITDA improved from 5.47x at the end of 2025 to 4.45x on a last-twelve-months basis at 30 September 2026, and net debt to reported EBITDA from 4.84x to 3.91x. Of the improvement in total leverage, 77.10% came from higher EBITDA and 22.90% from lower debt, chiefly USD 95.0 million of voluntary term loan prepayments. On the issuer's adjusted measure total leverage moved from 4.71x to 4.09x, a smaller step, because reported EBITDA grew 17.76% against 10.37% for adjusted EBITDA as the charges the issuer adds back shrank. The adjusted ratios are therefore the better guide to underlying progress and the reported ratios the better guide to the cost actually incurred.

Basis: calculation C09; calculation C18; calculation C19; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 102; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 12; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 40

The FY2024 ratios of 25.77x total debt and 23.75x net debt to reported EBITDA and cover of 1.26x should not be read as a trend point. Sterling Check was acquired on 31 October 2024, so the year-end balance sheet carries all of the acquisition debt while the income statement holds only two months of the acquired earnings and transaction charges of USD 125.7 million. FY2025 is the first full year of the combined business, and the 9M 2025 and 9M 2026 stubs both include Sterling for nine months, which is why the last-twelve-months construction is comparable. The issuer gives pro forma revenue and net loss for FY2024 and FY2023 but no pro forma EBITDA, so a like-for-like FY2024 leverage cannot be built from the filings.

Basis: calculation C05; calculation C09; calculation C19; 10-K_2024-12-31_fa-20241231.htm.jsonl, page 136; 10-K_2024-12-31_fa-20241231.htm.jsonl, page 155; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 102; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 153

Cash interest cover rose from 2.35x in FY2025 to 3.17x on a last-twelve-months basis, and from 2.73x to 3.45x on adjusted EBITDA. Cash interest paid is 12.72% lower than in FY2025, which fits the issuer's explanation that term loan interest fell after the margin was reduced on 30 July 2025 to 2.50% to 2.75% over SOFR and after voluntary prepayments of USD 95.0 million in 2026. Interest expense, net understates the cash cost in 2026 because it is net of unrealised swap gains and interest income, so cover should be read on cash interest paid. Cover would fall again if SOFR rose, because the hedges are partial: swaps cover 48.77% of principal today and 26.00% after the three swaps maturing on 31 December 2026 expire, leaving 74.00% of the principal exposed to SOFR.
Basis: calculation C09; calculation C16; calculation C23; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 156; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 12–13

Cash generation is adequate but thinner than adjusted EBITDA suggests. Last-twelve-months operating cash flow is 51.89% of adjusted EBITDA and levered free cash flow is 36.39%, after cash interest, cash taxes that rose 67.50% in the nine months, working capital absorption and capital expenditure that rose 56.85% on higher capitalized software. Levered free cash flow equals 8.90% of total debt. In the nine months to 30 September 2026, term loan prepayments absorbed 74.11% of levered free cash flow and share repurchases a further 29.94%, so together they used 104.05% and cash stayed flat. The USD 100.0 million repurchase programme authorised on 25 February 2026 remains partly unused, so shareholder distributions compete directly with deleveraging for the same cash.

Basis: calculation C13; calculation C19; calculation C20; calculation C21; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 3–4; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 48; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 50

Liquidity is comfortable against near-term obligations. Cash of USD 240.9 million and an undrawn revolver of USD 249.3 million give USD 490.2 million. The year-end ladder shows no scheduled principal in 2026 or 2027, the first instalment falls in 2028, the undrawn revolver matures on 31 October 2029 and the term loan on 31 October 2031, so no funded principal is due before 2028 and the final maturity is five years away. The one large cash call outside the ladder is discretionary: the acquisition of 4 November 2026, of which USD 45.0 million was drawn on the revolver and USD 80.0 million came from sources the filing does not state.

Basis: calculation C06; calculation C08; calculation C19; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 157; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 11–12; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 23; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 45

The acquisition raises net debt by up to the full cash consideration of USD 125.0 million. On unchanged last-twelve-months EBITDA this lifts net leverage from 3.91x to 4.19x, which gives back part of the improvement since the end of 2025 until the acquired earnings, which the filing does not state, are counted. The figure is an upper bound because cash acquired and the working-capital settlement are not stated, and it is not cumulative with any later event.
Basis: calculation C10; calculation C19; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 23

Claims outside funded debt are small. Operating lease liabilities are USD 8,763 thousand and the accrued legal liability is USD 8.5 million at 30 September 2026, and deferred revenues of USD 4.8 million are too small to act as a funding float. No pension, retiree medical, factoring or supply-chain finance obligation was found. Two items have no stated amount: the minimum-volume purchase commitment under a twelve-month service contract, which management expects to exceed in the ordinary course, and the compliance duties under consent decrees with the US Federal Trade Commission inherited from a 2013 acquisition.

Basis: calculation C19; calculation C22; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 19; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 33; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 112

The strongest evidence against the improving trend is that earnings growth, not cash generation, explains most of it. Levered free cash flow converts only 36.39% of adjusted EBITDA, debt prepayments and share repurchases together took more than all of it in the nine months, and the acquisition adds debt before it adds reported earnings. The improvement would be confirmed if net leverage on reported EBITDA stayed below the 4.84x of the end of 2025 once the acquisition is consolidated and cover stayed above 2.35x. It would be reversed by a further debt-funded acquisition or a larger repurchase programme absorbing free cash flow, or by a rise in SOFR while 74.00% of principal is unhedged.
Basis: calculation C09; calculation C10; calculation C20; calculation C21; calculation C23

A hiring slowdown is the credible initiating condition, because most revenue is pre-onboarding screening that depends on hiring volumes. Lower volumes would first reduce revenue and the operating leverage that has lifted Adjusted EBITDA margin, then cut EBITDA faster than cash interest, which does not fall with volumes, so cover would narrow first, prepayments would shrink next and net leverage would rise last. The observable triggers are quarterly revenue growth, Adjusted EBITDA margin and whether the repurchase programme continues. No stress figure is established here.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 32; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 40; calculation C09; calculation C21

Data quality is good where it can be tested. Every balance sheet, cash flow and income identity reconciles exactly across the periods, segment revenues and Adjusted EBITDA add to the totals, and the FY2024 figures agree between the two annual reports. The main definitional risk is that the issuer states no unadjusted EBITDA, so the reported ratios rest on a derived measure and are shown beside the issuer-adjusted ratios. Further limits are that security and guarantees are described only in the 2024 annual report, that the last printed maturity table is dated 31 December 2025, and that no discrete quarters are supplied, which limits any reading of seasonality.
Basis: calculation C03; calculation C04; calculation C11; calculation C12; calculation C14; 10-K_2024-12-31_fa-20241231.htm.jsonl, page 112; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 157

## Findings
### Bottom line

Silver Lake's control, at 51.4% with an approval right over debt above USD 100.0 million, makes financial policy a sponsor decision, and the record since 2023 mixes debt repayment with acquisitions and cash returns, so creditors cannot rely on steady deleveraging.

The operating business is the stronger credit point: a broad customer base, no customer at 10% of FY2025 revenues and gross retention of about 96%, set against revenue that follows hiring volumes and a regulatory regime that includes consent decrees. Sponsor and governance risk is medium: no related-party payments or sponsor fees are disclosed, but cash was paid out in 2023 and acquisitions continue.
### Key findings

Silver Lake control decides financial policy, and its consent right is a sponsor check, not a creditor protection. Silver Lake beneficially owned 51.4% of the common stock at the end of 2025, down from 51.7% a year earlier, and under the stockholders' agreement its approval is needed for debt above USD 100.0 million, joint ventures above USD 100.0 million and a change of control for as long as it holds at least 25%. A large debt-funded acquisition or recapitalisation therefore cannot happen without the sponsor, so financial policy follows the sponsor's view. Creditors rely on the credit agreement for protection, and that agreement is not supplied, so capacity to pay out cash, move assets or prime lenders is not assessed.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 72; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 73; 10-K_2024-12-31_fa-20241231.htm.jsonl, page 73; calculation B06

Documented sponsor behaviour is mixed, not adverse. The only large payout was the USD 217.7 million special dividend of August 2023, equal to 133.73% of that year's operating cash flow and paid from cash without any borrowing, before the Sterling acquisition. Since the acquisition the company has made voluntary term loan prepayments of USD 65.0 million in 2025 and USD 95.0 million in the nine months to September 2026, says it expects to pay no dividends, and has authorised a USD 100.0 million repurchase programme that excludes shares held by SLP Fastball Aggregator, L.P. and its affiliates, whom the filing does not describe further. No management fees, monitoring fees or related-party payments are disclosed, though the proxy statement that would show them is not supplied.

Acquisitions are a repeated strategy, so integration and funding risk recurs. Infinite ID was bought for USD 41.0 million in September 2023, Sterling in October 2024 at a value of about USD 2.2 billion, with 22.30% paid in stock and the rest in cash funded from cash on hand and a new term loan of USD 2,185.0 million, and a data platform business on 4 November 2026 for USD 125.0 million in cash with USD 45.0 million drawn on the revolver. Each deal brings integration cost, with transaction charges of USD 125.7 million in FY2024 and integration expense of USD 18.1 million in FY2025. The latest deal is small at 5.69% of Sterling's consideration, but it followed USD 95.0 million of paydown, so creditors should expect leverage to rise again when a suitable target appears, and the target, its earnings and the funding of the other USD 80.0 million are not stated.

The business is a high-retention, transactional screening franchise whose revenue still moves with hiring. Gross retention was about 96% in both 2024 and 2025, the customer count stayed in the tens of thousands in both years, and no customer reached 10% of FY2025 revenues, although one customer was about 12% in FY2024 and FY2023. Against that, most revenue is pre-onboarding screening ordered per individual, contracts carry no minimum volumes and customers can leave on short notice without penalty, so a hiring slowdown lowers revenue without any contract being lost. The annual reports state customers, retention, tenure and screens for both years, which corrects the earlier view in Financial foundation that no such series is stated; two years show stable retention but are too short to show a trend.

Revenue is concentrated by country and split almost evenly between the legacy and acquired businesses. The United States generated 85.81% of FY2025 revenues, and Sterling supplied 49.07% of gross segment revenues against 44.30% for First Advantage Americas and 6.62% for First Advantage International. The International segment is the weak part: its revenues fell 6.17% in the nine months to September 2026 and its Adjusted EBITDA margin dropped to 5.95% from 16.12%, so it adds little cushion.

Regulatory and legal exposure is structural but contained today. The company remains bound by consent decrees with the US Federal Trade Commission inherited from a 2013 acquisition, requiring compliance with consumer-reporting law and a biennially audited security programme, and it carries an accrued legal liability of USD 8.5 million. A breach would add cost or restrict products, but the filings document no breach.

Governance disclosure is strong where it is audited and thin where it is incorporated by reference. Statements are audited, with an opinion that they present fairly, and internal control was effective, quarterly reports are filed and no material related-party transactions are reported, but directors, pay and independence sit in a proxy statement that is not supplied. Overall, First Advantage presents medium sponsor and governance risk: the key supported behaviours are the 2023 payout and repeated acquisitions, which matter because they move cash and debt at the sponsor's discretion, and imply that deleveraging is a choice, not a commitment. Countervailing evidence is the voluntary paydown and the stated policy of no dividends. Further analysis requires the proxy statement and the credit agreement.
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against reading sponsor behaviour as mixed, not adverse, is the 2023 special dividend, paid to shareholders of whom Silver Lake is the largest, and the speed with which a new acquisition followed the 2026 paydown; together they suggest cash is returned or redeployed whenever liquidity allows. The view would turn adverse if the company announced a debt-funded dividend or buyback, if a new amendment widened sponsor consent to higher leverage, or if the credit agreement proved to allow wide payouts or asset transfers. It would improve if the proxy statement showed no sponsor fees or related-party payments, if the 2026 target proved modest and low-risk, and if voluntary prepayments continued at the 2026 pace. A fall in Silver Lake's holding below 25% would remove its approval rights and change who decides debt questions.

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

First Advantage completed the acquisition of Sterling Check Corp. on 31 October 2024. The transaction valued Sterling at about USD 2.2 billion and was paid with cash on hand, new debt and common stock: Sterling's holders received about USD 1,168.1 million in cash and shares with a fair value of USD 494.6 million, and Sterling's own debt was repaid. At closing the company refinanced its existing credit agreement into a first lien facility with a term loan of USD 2,185.0 million due in 2031 and a USD 250.0 million revolver due in 2029, which is the only funded debt.

The company prepaid USD 65.0 million of the term loan in 2025 and USD 95.0 million in the nine months to September 2026, with no penalties.

Effective 4 November 2026 the company acquired a U.S.-based data platform business and a small employment background screening operation for USD 125.0 million in cash, subject to working-capital adjustments, and borrowed USD 45.0 million on the revolver. spans.text: ## Request

First Advantage Corp (issuer fa-1210677), as of 2026-11-18, credit snapshot pathway. Scope: fundamental credit synthesis built on Source readiness, Financial foundation and Business & governance, covering business risk, cash-flow durability, liquidity, leverage, refinancing capacity, sponsor policy and the main downside path.
## Sources

Document dates are the dates each report states it was signed; no document states a filing date. No external source was used. Figures from the supplied analyses are carried unchanged.
## Findings
### Bottom line

First Advantage's credit profile is adequate and improving but still levered: net leverage is 3.91x last-twelve-months reported EBITDA, or 4.19x pro forma for the 4 November 2026 acquisition, so creditors rely on earnings growth and the sponsor's restraint rather than on a cushion.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation F01

The supports are a sticky customer base, USD 490.2 million of liquidity with no principal due before 2028 and cash interest cover of 3.17x. The constraints are hiring-driven revenue without minimum volumes, floating-rate debt with 74.00% unhedged after 2026, thin free cash flow conversion and a controlling sponsor that has paid out cash and keeps buying businesses. Cash after the acquisition is not established.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation F01; calculation F02; calculation F03; calculation F05; calculation F07
### Key findings

The credit is adequate and improving, but leverage is still close to four times EBITDA. Total debt to reported EBITDA fell from 5.47x at the end of 2025 to 4.45x on the last twelve months to 30 September 2026, and net debt to reported EBITDA from 4.84x to 3.91x at 30 September 2026, which becomes 4.19x pro forma for the acquisition of 4 November 2026. Of the improvement in total leverage, 77.10% came from higher EBITDA and 22.90% from lower debt, and on the issuer's adjusted measure total leverage moved from 4.71x to 4.09x. The pro forma figure counts the full cash consideration and no earnings from the target, so it is an upper bound, and pro forma cash is not established.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation F01; calculation F04

Liquidity is the strongest support. Cash of USD 240.9 million and an undrawn revolver of USD 249.3 million give USD 490.2 million, 24.62% of total debt, and no scheduled principal falls due before 2028, with the revolver due in October 2029 and the term loan in October 2031. The acquisition of 4 November 2026 used part of this buffer, and the cash that remains after it is not established.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation F02

Cash flow covers interest comfortably but converts only about a third of adjusted EBITDA into free cash flow. Reported EBITDA covers cash interest 3.17x, up from 2.35x at the end of 2025, but last-twelve-months levered free cash flow is 36.39% of adjusted EBITDA and 8.90% of total debt, after cash taxes that rose 67.50% and capital expenditure that rose 56.85% in the nine months to September 2026. Prepayments and share repurchases together used 104.05% of nine-month free cash flow, so deleveraging is funded by free cash flow only if buybacks and deals do not take more.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation F01; calculation F03

Business risk is moderate: customers are sticky but revenue follows hiring. Gross retention was about 96% in both 2024 and 2025 and no customer reached 10% of FY2025 revenues, but most revenue is pre-onboarding screening ordered per individual, contracts carry no minimum volumes and customers can leave at short notice. The United States produces 85.81% of revenues, Sterling now supplies 49.07% of gross segment revenues, and the International segment, whose revenues fell 6.17% in the nine months with a margin of 5.95% against 16.12%, adds little cushion.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation F07

Rate risk is a real constraint on the improvement. Interest is floating, three swaps mature on 31 December 2026, and 74.00% of principal is unhedged after that date, so a rise in SOFR would lift cash interest. The issuer estimated that a 100 bp move changes twelve months of interest on the first lien facility by about USD 21.1 million, which is 14.94% of last-twelve-months cash interest paid; it does not say whether the swaps are in that estimate.
Basis: calculation F05; calculation F08; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 118; Financial foundation (CP-1)

Sponsor control makes financial policy the swing factor. Silver Lake holds 51.4% and must approve debt above USD 100.0 million while it holds 25% or more. The record is mixed: a USD 217.7 million special dividend in 2023, voluntary prepayments of USD 65.0 million in 2025 and USD 95.0 million in the nine months to September 2026, a USD 100.0 million repurchase programme and three acquisitions in three years, the latest for USD 125.0 million with USD 45.0 million drawn on the revolver. Deleveraging is therefore a choice and not a commitment.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation F07

Information gaps keep several conclusions provisional. No rating, market quote, executed credit agreement or proxy statement is supplied and the 2026 target is unnamed, so market access, covenant capacity and post-deal leverage are judged on reported figures only.
Basis: Source readiness (CP-0); Business & governance (CP-1A)
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against an adequate and improving credit is that part of the improvement comes from lower one-off charges and part is already reversed by the acquisition. Reported EBITDA grew 17.76% against 10.37% for adjusted EBITDA because the charges the issuer adds back shrank, free cash flow converts only 36.39% of adjusted EBITDA, and the acquisition of 4 November 2026 lifts net leverage to 4.19x pro forma from 3.91x before any earnings from the target are counted. The view would be confirmed if net leverage stayed below the 4.84x of end-2025 once the acquisition is consolidated and cover stayed above 2.35x. It would turn negative if reported EBITDA fell 13.43% on a pro forma net debt basis, which returns net leverage to 4.84x, or 25.84%, which returns cover to 2.35x, or if a further debt-funded deal or payout used the liquidity.
Basis: calculation F01; calculation F03; calculation F04; calculation F06; Financial foundation (CP-1)
### Limitations

- No rating, market price or peer set is available, so the conclusion on refinancing capacity rests on maturity profile and leverage alone and could be too optimistic or too cautious about market access.
Basis: Source readiness (CP-0); 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 69

- Cash and liquidity after the 4 November 2026 acquisition are not established, so the liquidity conclusion describes the position at 30 September 2026 and may overstate the buffer, because the part of the consideration not drawn on the revolver is paid from cash.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 23

- Without an executed credit agreement the springing test and the terms of any restricted-payment or asset-transfer baskets are known only from the issuer's summary, so no covenant headroom is assessed and the liquidity conclusion assumes the revolver stays fully available.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 12; Source readiness (CP-0)
- No management case or guidance is supplied, so the outlook is qualitative and its direction could change with a company forecast.
Basis: Source readiness (CP-0)
### Company description

First Advantage sells employment background screening and identity verification to employers, covering criminal, education and work-history checks, identity and drug screening, driver and healthcare credentials, continuous monitoring and adjacent products such as fleet compliance and hiring tax credits. Revenue is transactional, since an employer orders a package of checks for one person, so it follows hiring volumes, yet relationships are long, gross retention is about 96% and no customer reached 10% of FY2025 revenues. The United States produces 85.81% of revenues and the Sterling acquisition of October 2024 made Sterling 49.07% of gross segment revenues. For creditors this means cash-flow visibility is good at the relationship level and weak at the volume level, so debt service depends on earnings tracking hiring and refinancing confidence rests on leverage, not on contracted revenue.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation F07
### Ownership and group structure

Silver Lake beneficially owns 51.4% of the common stock and holds approval rights over debt above USD 100.0 million, joint ventures above USD 100.0 million and change of control while it keeps 25% or more. The listed registrant is a holding company with no liabilities of its own, and the debt sits at First Advantage Holdings, LLC, guaranteed by its direct parent and material wholly owned domestic restricted subsidiaries according to the 2024 annual report, which is the only filing to describe the guarantee and collateral. Restricted-group figures are not supplied, so structural subordination to non-guarantor subsidiaries is not sized. Leverage tolerance has been shown by the 2024 acquisition financing and then by USD 160.0 million of voluntary prepayments over 2025 and the nine months to 2026-09-30, while payout behaviour is a 2023 special dividend and a 2026 repurchase programme.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2024-12-31_fa-20241231.htm.jsonl, page 158; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 174–175; calculation F07
### Revenue drivers and pricing power

Revenue is driven by volumes: most revenue is pre-onboarding screening that follows employer hiring, growth in the nine months to September 2026 came from existing customers at 8.4% and new customers at 4.2%, and the issuer says pricing was relatively stable, so pricing power is not demonstrated. Revenue is recurring in relationship but not in volume, because contracts carry no minimum volumes and customers can end them at short notice. It is cyclical with hiring and exposed to customers taking screening in-house or using AI-driven hiring tools. That means a hiring slowdown reduces revenue without any contract being lost, which is the first break in the downside path.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation F09; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 39; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 34
### Cost structure and margin resilience

Cost of services, which is mostly third-party data, government fees, fulfilment and customer care, is 54.33% of FY2025 revenues, so a large part of cost varies with volume and protects margin when orders fall. The issuer says third-party fees are typically invoiced to customers as pass-through costs, but its risk factors state that fee increases cannot always be passed on, so pass-through is partial. Adjusted EBITDA margin was 28.5% in the nine months to September 2026 against 28.1% a year earlier, with automation and operating leverage credited by management, while the International segment margin fell to 5.95% from 16.12%. Margins can be defended against a moderate volume fall, but technology and overhead costs are largely fixed, so a deeper fall would cut EBITDA faster than revenue.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation F04; calculation F07; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 41; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 90
### Capital intensity and FCF conversion

The business needs little physical capital but invests continuously in software, and capital expenditure, mostly capitalized software, rose 56.85% in the nine months to September 2026. Last-twelve-months operating cash flow is 51.89% of adjusted EBITDA and levered free cash flow 36.39%, after cash interest, cash taxes that rose 67.50% and working-capital outflow as revenue grew. The issuer does not split maintenance and growth capital expenditure, so the capex that could be cut in a downturn is not established. EBITDA therefore translates into positive but modest free cash flow, 8.90% of total debt, which supports debt service and some deleveraging but not rapid repayment.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation F03
### Porter's five forces

Rivalry is moderate to high: the market is fragmented, with a limited number of multinational firms, and the issuer competes on accuracy, turnaround, compliance and price, so competitors can force price concessions that would cut margin. New entrants are a live threat from applicant tracking and payroll providers that build screening into their products, which could erode volumes and the integrations that sustain retention. Substitutes are customers insourcing screening and AI-driven hiring tools that lower hiring volumes. Buyer power is high, because customers can leave at short notice, buy from several providers and are often steered by human capital software partners. Supplier power is meaningful, since data providers and laboratories are non-exclusive, some are owned by competitors, and fee increases cannot always be passed on, which pressures margin at the cost-of-services line.
### PEST analysis

Regulatory and economic factors are material and the others are covered under competition. Consumer-reporting law, state fair-chance laws and privacy laws shape which checks customers may use, and the company remains bound by consent decrees with the US Federal Trade Commission, so a compliance failure would add cost or restrict products; the accrued legal liability is USD 8.5 million. The hiring cycle is the economic driver of volumes, and floating-rate debt makes interest rates the second economic factor.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 27; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 33; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 19; calculation F05; calculation F07
### SWOT analysis

- Strengths: retention of about 96% and a broad customer base; USD 490.2 million of liquidity with no principal due before 2028; positive levered free cash flow; scale as one of a limited number of multinational providers.
- Weaknesses: leverage near four times EBITDA with floating rates; revenue tied to hiring without minimum volumes; thin free cash flow conversion; sponsor control and an acquisitive record.
- Opportunities: continued voluntary paydown and earnings growth could bring leverage lower, and identity-verification and monitoring products add recurring-type revenue according to management.
- Threats: a hiring slowdown, in-sourcing and AI-driven hiring tools, regulatory action, SOFR rising once swaps expire, and a further debt-funded acquisition or payout.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation F01; calculation F02; calculation F03; calculation F05; calculation F07
### Strengths and weaknesses

The strongest credit support is a sticky, broad customer base, because gross retention of about 96% and the absence of any customer at 10% of revenue steady cash flow and make a sudden revenue loss unlikely; the implication is better debt-service visibility than the transactional contracts alone suggest. Second, earnings growth and voluntary prepayments have cut leverage, lifting cover to 3.17x. Third, USD 490.2 million of liquidity with no principal before 2028 gives time to absorb a downturn. Fourth, levered free cash flow is positive at 8.90% of total debt.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation F01; calculation F02; calculation F03; calculation F07

The main weaknesses are, first, leverage of 3.91x net, or 4.19x pro forma for the acquisition of 4 November 2026, with 74.00% of principal floating and unhedged after 2026, which makes interest cost and leverage sensitive to rates and earnings. Second, a sponsor-controlled financial policy with a record of a payout and repeated acquisitions means cash and debt can move away from creditors. Third, revenue follows hiring and contracts carry no minimum volumes, so a downturn cuts revenue and EBITDA quickly. Fourth, free cash flow is only 36.39% of adjusted EBITDA while capital spending and cash taxes rise.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation F01; calculation F03; calculation F05; calculation F07
### Financial profile and credit quality

Scale and market position are average, with revenue large enough to rank among the few multinational providers but a fragmented market. Competitive advantage is average: integrations with human capital platforms, proprietary data and 96% retention are offset by short-notice termination and entrants. Diversification is average, with a broad customer base and no concentration but one service line, one country at 85.81% and hiring-driven demand. Cost and capex flexibility is average, since variable cost of services helps but software spending is rising. Margin stability is average and free cash flow stability average, with a negative levered free cash flow year in the acquisition period and a positive trend since. The ability to refinance is average with low confidence because no rating or market data exist and no principal falls due before 2028. Liquidity is strong at USD 490.2 million before the acquisition. Financial policy and governance is average, weighed down by sponsor control but helped by a stated no-dividend policy and voluntary paydown. The main supports are liquidity, retention and the deleveraging trend; the constraints are leverage, rate exposure and hiring sensitivity; the trend is improving; the missing datapoints are the credit agreement, ratings and the 2026 target.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); Source readiness (CP-0); calculation F01; calculation F02; calculation F03; calculation F07
### Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds

Over twelve to twenty-four months the tailwinds are continued earnings growth, lower interest from the 2025 repricing and 2026 prepayments, and no principal due before 2028; the headwinds are the expiry of swaps on 31 December 2026, integration and funding of the 2026 acquisition, and any weakening of hiring. Over three to five years the first scheduled instalment falls in 2028, the revolver matures in October 2029 and the term loan in October 2031, so refinancing arrives only if leverage has not fallen. Management cites identity fraud, contingent workforces and analytics as sector tailwinds; headwinds are in-sourcing, AI-driven hiring tools, privacy and fair-chance rules and competition. No company guidance is supplied, so the outlook is qualitative.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation F02; calculation F05; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 13–15; 10-K_2025-12-31_fa-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 39
### Downside scenario

The initiating condition is a hiring slowdown across retail, transportation and healthcare customers. Orders fall at once because contracts carry no minimum volumes, revenue follows, and EBITDA falls faster than revenue because technology and overhead costs are largely fixed, while cost of services at 54.33% of revenue flexes. Cash interest does not fall with volumes and rises if SOFR rises after the swaps expire, so cover narrows first: a 25.84% fall in reported EBITDA returns cover to 2.35x. Free cash flow then shrinks and prepayments slow, so net leverage rises, and a fall of 13.43% on pro forma net debt returns it to the 4.84x of end-2025. Management levers are to stop buybacks and acquisitions, defer software capex and keep prepaying; liquidity of USD 490.2 million before the acquisition and no principal due before 2028 mean resilience appears sufficient to avoid distress in this scenario, though the buffer and the revolver covenant test above 40.0% use must be watched. Observable triggers are screening volumes, adjusted EBITDA margin, cash after the acquisition and any new payout.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation F01; calculation F02; calculation F03; calculation F05; calculation F06; 10-Q_2026-09-30_fa-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 12
### Overall credit view

Overall, First Advantage presents an adequate business profile supported by sticky customers, scale among multinational screening firms and ample liquidity, but credit quality is constrained by leverage near four times EBITDA, floating-rate exposure, hiring-driven volumes and a controlling sponsor with an acquisitive record. Cash-flow durability appears adequate: interest is covered 3.17x and free cash flow is positive, but conversion is thin. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on leverage at 2028 and later maturities and on whether the sponsor keeps using cash for deals. The primary downside path is a hiring slowdown that cuts EBITDA faster than revenue while rates rise on unhedged debt. Further analysis would require the credit agreement, ratings and market data, the target and cash after the 2026 acquisition, and the proxy statement.
